_what: Published predictions for Planet Nine's orbit and physical properties. Drives the Designer page, the 'put the planet anywhere' scoring, and the physical-properties panel.
_caution: These are model inferences, not measurements. No object has been detected. Ranges differ between papers because they assume different ETNO samples and different treatments of survey bias.
_provenance: Every field carries a `src` tag: 'abstract' = quoted verbatim from the paper's abstract; 'paper' = read out of the paper's body or figures; 'derived' = computed by us from quoted values; 'ours' = our own interpolation or assumption, NOT a published number. Checked October 2026.

orbit_predictions.label: Batygin & Brown 2016

src.e: paper (Brown & Batygin 2021 sec. 6 describes the original choice as m=10, e=0.7, i=30, 'merely notional')

orbit_predictions.note: The founding paper. Its abstract gives only a mass floor and the fact that the planet's perihelion is 180 degrees from the minor bodies'; the specific orbit was a proof-of-concept, not a fit.

orbit_predictions.label: Brown & Batygin 2016 (observational constraints)

src.e_range_derived: derived from the quoted a and q ranges

orbit_predictions.note: Also the source of the first exclusion result: comparison with surveys ruled out roughly two-thirds of the orbit, and placed the planet likely near aphelion.

orbit_predictions.label: Millholland & Laughlin 2017
orbit_predictions.note: Constrained by requiring mean-motion resonances with the known ETNOs. Note that its node and longitude of perihelion differ substantially from Brown & Batygin's.

orbit_predictions.label: Batygin, Adams, Brown & Becker 2019 (review)
orbit_predictions.note: The Physics Reports review. Also notes the clustering it explains is for a > ~250 AU.

orbit_predictions.label: Brown & Batygin 2021 (headline values)
orbit_predictions.note: The most-quoted numbers. The abstract gives NO longitude of perihelion and NO ascending node, so this set alone cannot place the planet on the sky.

orbit_predictions.label: Brown & Batygin 2021 (marginalized posterior)
orbit_predictions.note: Same paper, full posterior medians. These differ from the headline values above, and they are the only published set that includes both angles, so the site's sky track uses this one. Their Figure 9 puts the sky-density peak near RA 45 deg; the median orbit here has its aphelion near RA 67 deg. Those are different quantities (a density peak over the whole posterior versus one orbit), so they are not in conflict, but do not present either as 'the' predicted position.

orbit_predictions.label: Phan et al. 2025 (IRAS/AKARI far-IR candidate)
orbit_predictions.note: One candidate surviving selection and image inspection, out of 13 pairs. Two epochs cannot determine an orbit; the authors call for follow-up. Not a detection.

orbit_predictions.label: Brown, Holman & Batygin 2024 (after the searches)
orbit_predictions.note: Brown, Holman & Batygin's update after ZTF, DES and PS1 ruled out 78% of the 2021 predictions: medians of the reference population still standing, with the 15.8 and 84.1 percentiles as the uncertainties (sec. 6, read from the arXiv HTML of arXiv:2401.17977 on 2026-11-20; the PDF text had garbled them). The other orbital elements 'remain generally unchanged'.

search_exclusions._what: How much of the predicted parameter space has actually been searched. These are the hard numbers for 'why hasn't anyone found it'.
search_exclusions.remaining_space: Faint (V > 21) and concentrated near and in the region where the northern galactic plane crosses the ecliptic. The discussion adds a smaller region in the poorly covered southern galactic plane and a strip below declination -30, and says Rubin's survey 'will be sensitive to all but the faintest and most northern predicted positions'.
search_exclusions.src: Brown, Holman & Batygin 2024, abstract and discussion (read 2026-11-20)

physical_properties._source: Linder & Mordasini 2016 (A&A 589:A134) thermal-evolution models, plus the albedo range adopted by Brown & Batygin 2021.
physical_properties._caution: Linder & Mordasini's published grid is for 5, 10, 20 and 50 Earth masses at 280, 700 and 1120 AU. Values quoted for a 6.2 Earth-mass planet at ~460 AU are OUR interpolation between their grid points, not numbers they state.

linder_mordasini_anchor.note: T_eff of 47 K is far above the ~10 K equilibrium temperature: the planet is self-luminous.

brightness_model._what: How the site turns a planet's mass, distance and albedo into a V magnitude, a width and a temperature (charts/placeplanet.js), and how it decides whether the searches would have seen it.
brightness_model._choice: Two published radius rules disagree. Linder & Mordasini's interior models give 2.92, 3.66, 4.62 and 6.32 Earth radii for 5, 10, 20 and 50 Earth masses; Brown & Batygin's fit, and the 2024 search that tested it, use r = m/3, which is smaller (2.3 against about 3.2 Earth radii at 6.9 Earth masses, about 0.7 magnitude fainter). We use m/3, because a planet scored here is then judged by the same model that ruled out 78% of the predictions. Linder & Mordasini's grid is kept as the check on the magnitude formula and as the source of the temperature, which they model and Brown & Batygin do not.

radius_rule.src: paper (Brown & Batygin 2021 sec. 5 and Brown, Holman & Batygin 2024 sec. 3, both after Wu & Lithwick 2013)

albedo.src: paper (Neptune's geometric albedo, the nominal value in Linder & Mordasini 2016 sec. 2 after Traub & Oppenheimer 2010; Brown & Batygin 2021 call their lower bound of 0.2 'half that of Neptune')

magnitude_formula.formula: V = 5 log10(1329 km / (D sqrt(p))) + 5 log10(r (r - 1)), D the diameter in km, p the geometric albedo, r the distance from the Sun in AU, seen at opposition
magnitude_formula.src: derived (the standard reflected-light magnitude of a solar-system body)

check.src: derived; the published V is Linder & Mordasini 2016's abstract value, and the formula also gives their 5, 20 and 50 Earth-mass values (22.3, 21.3, 20.6) to within 0.12 magnitude

check_2024.src: derived; the published V is the median of the reference population the 2024 search left standing (Brown, Holman & Batygin 2024 sec. 6), at its median current distance and mass, which used albedos from 0.2 to 0.75

linder_mordasini_grid.src: paper (Linder & Mordasini 2016 sec. 4.3 and abstract; the temperatures hardly depend on distance from 5 to 1120 AU, sec. 5)

detection.src: paper (Brown, Holman & Batygin 2024 sec. 5: the combined ZTF, DES and PS1 searches are about 94% efficient brighter than V = 20.5, falling to 50% at V = 21.5)

hiding_rule.rule: the share of its orbital period the planet spends fainter than V_50pct
hiding_rule.src: ours (where on its orbit the planet is now is unknown, so each point of the orbit counts by the time spent there)

radius_earths.src: ours (interpolated from the Linder & Mordasini grid)

effective_temperature_k.src: ours (interpolated; their only quoted point is 47 K for 10 Earth masses at 700 AU)

albedo.src: paper (Brown & Batygin 2021 adopt 0.2 to 0.75; 0.2 is half Neptune's, 0.75 is pure Rayleigh scattering). The 'best' value is ours.
albedo.note: Brown & Batygin explicitly do not constrain albedo or diameter. A low albedo could make the planet ~3 magnitudes dimmer.

apparent_V_mag.src: abstract (Brown & Batygin 2016 give 22 < V < 25; the 2024 PS1 search says the surviving space is V > 21)

orbital_period_yr.src: derived (Kepler's third law from the a ranges above)

options: sub-Neptune (icy-rocky core with an H/He envelope)
composition.best: sub-Neptune (icy-rocky core with an H/He envelope)
composition.src: paper (Brown & Batygin 2021: 'for masses between 4-20 Mearth we assume that the most likely planetary composition is that of a sub-Neptune')

likely_appearance.note: No image exists and no paper predicts a colour. Methane in a cold H/He atmosphere would plausibly make it blue-cyan like Uranus and Neptune, but this is an extrapolation. Present it to users as an artist's choice, not a finding.

designer_slider_ranges._why: Min/max a user can dial in on the Designer page. Narrow slider = well constrained by the literature; wide slider = genuinely unknown. These bounds are ours, chosen to span the published predictions above with a little headroom.
